questions.question: What does the 2-norm condition number \(\kappa_2(A)\) of a nonsingular matrix quantify in the context of solving \(Ax=b\) with small perturbations in \(b\) and rounding errors?
questions.choice_A: The worst-case relative amplification of input perturbations in \(b\) into relative errors in the solution \(x\)
questions.choice_B: The average number of iterations required by conjugate gradients to solve \(Ax=b\)
questions.choice_C: The maximum possible absolute error in any component of \(x\)
questions.choice_D: The probability that Gaussian elimination without pivoting will fail

questions.question: Why are algorithms based on orthogonal transformations (e.g., Householder QR) regarded as numerically stable?
questions.choice_A: They minimize the Frobenius norm of the residual by construction
questions.choice_B: Orthogonal matrices have condition number 1 in the 2-norm and preserve vector norms, enabling backward-stable implementations
questions.choice_C: They avoid all rounding error accumulation by exact cancellation
questions.choice_D: They guarantee the smallest possible fill-in for any sparsity pattern

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes rounding error accumulation in staged matrix products \(A_1 A_2 \cdots A_k\)?
questions.choice_A: Errors cancel pairwise, so total error is independent of \(k\)
questions.choice_B: The total forward error depends only on the Frobenius norms of the factors
questions.choice_C: The accumulated error typically grows with the number of stages and is magnified by the conditioning of the intermediate products
questions.choice_D: Associating multiplications as \(((A_1A_2)A_3)\cdots\) always minimizes error regardless of conditioning

questions.question: Which property illustrates preservation under orthogonal transforms?
questions.choice_A: For any matrix \(A\), \(\|QA\|_F = \|A\|_2\) for orthogonal \(Q\)
questions.choice_B: For orthogonal \(Q\), \(\kappa_2(QA)=\kappa_F(A)\)
questions.choice_C: For orthogonal \(Q\), all singular values of \(QA\) are strictly less than those of \(A\)
questions.choice_D: For orthogonal \(Q\) and \(R\), \(\|QAR\|_2 = \|A\|_2\)

questions.question: How does ill-conditioning in the Jacobian or weight matrices of deep networks typically affect gradient-based optimization?
questions.choice_A: It induces vanishing or exploding gradients and causes slow, anisotropic progress (e.g., zig-zagging)
questions.choice_B: It guarantees faster convergence because large singular values accelerate descent
questions.choice_C: It has no effect once batch normalization is used
questions.choice_D: It only affects generalization, not optimization dynamics

questions.question: Which description best distinguishes forward and backward stability?
questions.choice_A: Forward stability measures implementation speed, while backward stability measures memory usage
questions.choice_B: Backward stability shows the algorithm solves a nearby problem exactly; forward stability bounds the difference between the computed and exact solutions of the original problem
questions.choice_C: Forward stability implies perfect preservation of spectral norms; backward stability implies zero pivot growth
questions.choice_D: They are equivalent notions for all linear algebra algorithms

questions.question: Which statement about conditioning of products is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: The 2-norm condition number is additive across products: \(\kappa_2(AB)=\kappa_2(A)+\kappa_2(B)\)
questions.choice_B: If \(A\) and \(B\) are well-conditioned, \(AB\) must be orthogonal
questions.choice_C: One has \(\kappa_2(AB) \le \kappa_2(A)\,\kappa_2(B)\); thus inserting orthogonal factors (with \(\kappa_2=1\)) does not worsen conditioning
questions.choice_D: The conditioning of \(AB\) depends only on \(B\)

questions.question: In Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization on ill-conditioned bases, why is reorthogonalization used?
questions.choice_A: To reduce the spectral radius of the matrix being factored
questions.choice_B: To lower the arithmetic complexity from \(\mathcal{O}(n^3)\) to \(\mathcal{O}(n^2)\)
questions.choice_C: To exactly recover the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix
questions.choice_D: To mitigate loss of orthogonality due to rounding errors, improving numerical stability at extra cost

questions.question: When composing many sparse factors in a linear transform, which practical technique helps maintain numerical stability without destroying sparsity?
questions.choice_A: Rescaling intermediate vectors or blocks to avoid overflow/underflow while preserving sparsity structure
questions.choice_B: Converting all sparse factors to dense form before multiplication
questions.choice_C: Randomly permuting rows after every multiplication
questions.choice_D: Eliminating all diagonal scaling to simplify the graph

questions.question: How do spectral norms relate to generalization and stability in deep networks?
questions.choice_A: They only affect training loss, not generalization
questions.choice_B: Bounding the spectral norm controls a layer’s Lipschitz constant, which can stabilize training and tighten generalization bounds
questions.choice_C: They are irrelevant when using ReLU activations
questions.choice_D: They determine the exact VC dimension of the network

questions.question: What is a common optimization pathology caused by an ill-conditioned Hessian in gradient descent?
questions.choice_A: Convergence to the global optimum in one step
questions.choice_B: Uniform progress in all directions
questions.choice_C: Slow, oscillatory progress with narrow curved valleys (zig-zagging) that benefit from preconditioning
questions.choice_D: Immediate divergence regardless of step size

questions.question: Why can pre- and post-multiplying a least-squares problem by orthogonal matrices be beneficial?
questions.choice_A: It reduces the residual below machine epsilon
questions.choice_B: It guarantees that the condition number decreases
questions.choice_C: It changes the minimizer to a better-fitting solution
questions.choice_D: It preserves 2-norm conditioning and residual geometry while enabling numerically stable factorization steps

questions.question: Which floating-point error model is commonly used to reason about rounding in numerical linear algebra?
questions.choice_A: Each elementary operation satisfies \(\operatorname{fl}(a \circ b) = (a \circ b)(1+\delta)\) with \(|\delta| \le u\), where \(u\) is unit roundoff
questions.choice_B: Rounding errors are uniformly distributed in \([-1,1]\) regardless of magnitude
questions.choice_C: Errors are independent of the number of operations performed
questions.choice_D: Rounding errors cancel out exactly over long sequences of operations

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes the role of pivoting in Gaussian elimination with respect to stability and conditioning?
questions.choice_A: Pivoting reduces the condition number of the matrix
questions.choice_B: Partial pivoting helps achieve backward stability on a wide class of matrices without changing the intrinsic conditioning of the problem
questions.choice_C: No pivoting is needed if the matrix is sparse
questions.choice_D: Complete pivoting always produces an orthogonal factorization

questions.question: When designing factorizations as products of many sparse transforms (e.g., butterfly, wavelet, or graph-based), what trade-off is central for numerical stability?
questions.choice_A: Maximizing fill-in to better approximate dense matrices
questions.choice_B: Using larger step sizes during training
questions.choice_C: Balancing sparsity and ordering to limit fill-in and rounding error while keeping factors well-conditioned
questions.choice_D: Avoiding any rescaling to keep the model interpretable

questions.question: Which invariance property explains why orthogonal changes of basis do not alter the difficulty (conditioning) of least-squares problems in the 2-norm?
questions.choice_A: Orthogonal transforms minimize the Frobenius norm of any matrix
questions.choice_B: Orthogonal transforms equalize all singular values
questions.choice_C: Orthogonal transforms commute with any symmetric matrix
questions.choice_D: Orthogonal transforms preserve 2-norms and singular values, hence preserve \(\kappa_2\) and Lipschitz constants

questions.question: How do gradient clipping and spectral normalization differ as techniques for stabilizing training?
questions.choice_A: Clipping truncates gradient magnitudes post hoc, whereas spectral normalization constrains layer operator norms a priori
questions.choice_B: Both modify the loss landscape identically
questions.choice_C: Clipping increases the model’s Lipschitz constant while spectral normalization decreases it
questions.choice_D: Spectral normalization only affects bias terms

questions.question: In mixed-precision training, which practice helps maintain numerical stability without sacrificing most of the speed benefits?
questions.choice_A: Performing all computations in double precision
questions.choice_B: Using loss scaling and keeping critical reductions/normalizations (e.g., dot products, norm computations) in higher precision
questions.choice_C: Randomly zeroing gradients every few steps
questions.choice_D: Avoiding any use of batch normalization

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes problem conditioning from algorithmic stability?
questions.choice_A: A stable algorithm makes any problem well-conditioned
questions.choice_B: An ill-conditioned problem cannot be solved by any algorithm
questions.choice_C: An algorithm can be backward stable yet produce large forward errors if the underlying problem is ill-conditioned
questions.choice_D: Conditioning only matters for nonlinear problems

questions.question: What is a primary numerical benefit of initializing deep linear or orthogonal convolutional layers with orthogonal weights?
questions.choice_A: It guarantees zero training error
questions.choice_B: It forces all eigenvalues to be 1
questions.choice_C: It preserves the scale of signals and gradients across layers by keeping the singular values near 1
questions.choice_D: It eliminates the need for any normalization layers

questions.question: During Krylov subspace iterations (e.g., Lanczos), loss of orthogonality among basis vectors can corrupt spectral estimates. Which remedy is most directly targeted at this issue?
questions.choice_A: Reducing the time step
questions.choice_B: Increasing the batch size
questions.choice_C: Adding L2 weight decay
questions.choice_D: (Selective) reorthogonalization of basis vectors, possibly with modified Gram–Schmidt twice
